_Mean query latency (ms) of each retrieval strategy, per BEIR dataset and averaged across datasets (**Mean** row), alongside corpus size and mean query length (words, computed over the queries timed for that row). Fastest method per row in **bold**, second-fastest *italicised*._
<!-- END efficiency-table -->

Latency was measured on a single consumer machine: Apple MacBook Air (Mac14,15), M2 (4 performance + 4 efficiency cores, ARM64), 24 GB unified memory, macOS 26.5.2, no GPU involved. Every timed call goes through a stored query id, so it reuses the precomputed query embedding and measures database-side retrieval cost only, excluding model inference.

Read the two tables together and the trade-off the paper is about falls out. Binary Hamming search is the fastest method on seven of the eight datasets (NFCorpus, the smallest corpus, is the exception, where BM25 wins) — 22.9 ms averaged across datasets against BM25's 193.0 ms — and it costs between 0.001 and 0.031 nDCG@10 against the full-precision cosine ranking it approximates, with Touché the only dataset where that gap exceeds 0.011.

One cheap rerank stage on top closes almost all of it: `Hamming + cos_int8` is the second-fastest pipeline overall at 164.5 ms, comes within 0.004 nDCG@10 of `cos_float` on every dataset, and actually overtakes it on FiQA, Touché and TREC-COVID. Counting the MTEB baseline as a competing column, it is the best or second-best method of all fourteen on FiQA, SciDocs and TREC-COVID.

## Refreshing the results

```bash
python scripts/evaluation/effectiveness_md.py --measures nDCG@10 --inject README.md
python scripts/evaluation/efficiency_md.py --inject README.md
```

Each renderer rewrites its own `<!-- BEGIN … -->` / `<!-- END … -->` block and touches nothing else, so the two are independent and the order does not matter. Two caveats:

- The effectiveness table above is nDCG@10 only. Dropping `--measures nDCG@10` gives all four measures (AP, RR, P@10, nDCG@10) as four rows per dataset — 32 rows rather than 8.
- The **Query Length** column is computed from `data/datasets/beir/<dataset>/queries.jsonl`, which is not part of this repository. Without those files `efficiency_md.py` warns per dataset and drops the column from the regenerated table; the latency figures are unaffected.

## What `results/` holds

```
results/effectiveness/
  scores.csv              long format: dataset, method_key, method, measure, value
                          — all four measures, not just the nDCG@10 shown above
  table.tex               the paper's effectiveness table
  table.md                the block spliced in above
  heatmap_ndcg10.pdf      dataset × method heatmap of nDCG@10

results/efficiency/
  raw_timings.csv         every timed call
  per_query_means.csv     mean latency per (dataset, method, query)
  summary.csv             per (dataset, method) statistics
  overall_summary.csv     per method, across datasets
  table.tex               written by efficiency.py
  efficiency_table.tex    written by efficiency_table.py, with the two context columns
  efficiency_table.md     the block spliced in above
  bar_by_dataset.pdf      grouped bars, latency by dataset × method
  bar_overall.pdf         bars, latency by method, averaged across datasets
```
